en: The Sūtra on the Six Directions and the Rites of Śīkhaṇḍī, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a son of an elder named Śīkhaṇḍī.

Yuè rose early and groomed his hair; having bathed and put on patterned robes, he performed four prostrations facing east, four facing south, four facing west, four facing north, four toward the heavens, and four toward the earth.
When the Buddha entered the country for alms, he saw her from afar; he went to her house and asked her, "Why do you bow toward the six directions?
To what dharma does this correspond?"
Śikhālaputra said: "When my father was alive, he instructed me to perform prostrations toward six directions; I did not know what this meant.
Now that my father has passed away, I do not dare to disobey his instructions thereafter."
The Buddha said,
"Your father instructed you to bow in six directions, not to bow with your body.
Śīkhaṇḍī (Śikhāvala) then knelt and said:
“I pray that the Buddha will explain for me the meaning of these six directions of prostration.
The Buddha said, “Listen and take it to heart.”
If there are elders who are intelligent and capable of observing the four precepts without violation, they will be honored by others in this life and reborn in the heavens in future lives.
First, not killing any living beings; second, not stealing; third, not coveting the wives of others; and fourth, not engaging in false speech or double-tongued talk.
If the mind harbors lustful desire, anger, and delusion, one must restrain oneself and not yield to them.
One who cannot control these four mental states will have their ill repute heard of daily, just as the light gradually fades into darkness at the end of the month.
"One who is able to restrain their own malicious intent is like the new moon, whose light gradually brightens until it reaches the fullness of the fifteenth day.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are six matters by which wealth is daily diminished and exhausted."
First, taking pleasure in drinking alcohol;
second, taking pleasure in gambling;
third, taking pleasure in going to bed early and rising late.
Fourth, they delight in inviting guests and also desire others to invite them;
fifth, they delight in associating with evil companions;
sixth, they are arrogant and treat others with contempt.

Having committed the four grave evils mentioned above and further practicing these six matters, one obstructs one's own virtuous conduct; furthermore, one cannot even worry about managing one's livelihood, as wealth and property diminish day by day. What benefit would there be in bowing toward the six directions?
The Buddha said:
"There are four types of evil associates (pāpamitra):
first, those who harbor enmity within while outwardly pretending to be an associate."
Second, they speak pleasant words in the presence of others, but speak ill behind their backs;
third, when in urgent distress, they appear sorrowful in the presence of others, yet rejoice behind their backs;
fourth, they appear outwardly friendly and intimate, while inwardly they hatch schemes of malice.
Good spiritual friends also have four types:
first, those who appear outwardly like enemies but harbor deep inner intentions;
second, those who offer direct admonition in one's presence but speak of one's virtues to others.
Third, when someone is afflicted by illness or emaciated, or is being pressed by government officials with taxes and levies, one should relieve them of their distress.
Fourth, upon seeing those who are poor and lowly, one should not abandon them, but should instead contemplate seeking skillful means to bring them wealth.
Furthermore, there are four types of evil associates:
first, those who follow evildoers because they are difficult to admonish, instruct, or teach toward doing good;
second, those who follow drunkards because they are taught not to associate with those who delight in wine.
Third, teaching him to maintain self-restraint would have increased his affairs even further;
fourth, teaching him to take a worthy person as a friend, he therefore formed a close bond with Bo Yanzi.
Good spiritual friends also have four types:
first, those who help people who are impoverished and destitute to manage their livelihoods;
second, those who do not engage in disputes or competitive calculations with others.
Third, one should observe their comings and goings throughout the day;
fourth, one should maintain mindfulness of one another while sitting or rising.
Furthermore, there are four types of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra):
First, if someone is captured by officials, one shall take them back and hide them, subsequently resolving their case;
second, if someone is afflicted with illness or emaciation, one shall take them back to nurse and care for them;
third, if a friend or acquaintance dies, one shall provide a coffin and shroud for them.
Fourth, when a spiritual friend has passed away, one further keeps their family in mind.
Furthermore, there are four types of spiritual friends:
first, those who stop others when they wish to engage in conflict; [the other three follow].
Second, when they wish to follow evil associates, one should admonish and stop them;
third, when they do not wish to engage in livelihood, one should encourage and lead them to engage in livelihood;
fourth, when they take no pleasure in the Way of the Sūtras, one should instruct them so that they may come to believe in and rejoice in it.
Furthermore, there are four types of evil associates:
first, those who become greatly enraged at even a slight offense;
second, those who refuse to go when urgently requested to perform a task.
"Third, when seeing someone in distress, one avoids them and flees;
fourth, when seeing someone die, one abandons them and does not look upon them.
The Buddha said:
"Select those that are good and follow them; stay far away from those that are evil.
By associating with virtuous friends, one shall personally attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding those who bow facing east, this refers to a son serving his parents, for which there should be five matters:
first, he must attend to the management of the household;
second, he must rise early and instruct the servants and slaves to prepare meals at the proper time."
Third, one should not increase the anxieties of one’s parents;
fourth, one should constantly keep in mind the kindness of one’s parents;
fifth, when one’s parents are ill, one should be filled with apprehension and seek out physicians to treat them.
Parents have five matters regarding their children:
first, they should constantly mind them to leave evil and follow what is good;
second, they should teach them calculation and writing.
Third, one should teach them to uphold the sutras and precepts;
fourth, one should arrange for them to marry early;
fifth, one should provide them with everything they require from within the household.
"Regarding those who bow facing south, it refers to a disciple serving a teacher; there should be five matters:
first, one should respect and revere them;
second, one should be mindful of their kindness."
Third, one should follow whatever they are taught;
fourth, one should contemplate them without weariness;
fifth, one should praise them from behind.
The teacher’s instruction of disciples also consists of five matters:
first, one should cause them to understand quickly;
second, one should cause them to surpass the disciples of others.
Third, he desires to cause them to know and not forget;
fourth, he provides explanations for all doubts and difficulties;
fifth, he desires to cause his disciples' wisdom to surpass that of the teacher.
"Regarding those who bow facing west, this refers to the wife serving her husband, for which there are five matters:
first, when the husband returns from outside, she should rise to welcome him;
second, when the husband has gone out and is away, she should prepare the cooking, steam the food, and sweep the house to await his return."
Third, one must not harbor lustful thoughts toward men outside [the household], nor respond with insults when scolded by the husband, nor show resentment in one's facial expression;
fourth, one should follow the husband’s instructions and admonitions, and must not conceal any of the household goods;
fifth, one may only lie down to sleep after the husband has rested and secured the storerooms.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which a husband should treat his wife:
first, he should be respectful toward her when entering or leaving;
second, he should provide her with meals at the proper times and give her clothing and bedding.
Third, one should provide them with gold, silver, pearls, and jewels;
fourth, whatever is possessed within the household, whether much or little, should all be entrusted to them;
fifth, one must not keep concubines or attendants outside [the household] for improper purposes.
"Regarding those who bow facing north, it means that when one views one's relatives and friends, there should be five matters:
first, if one sees them committing evil deeds, one should go privately to a secluded place to admonish, enlighten, and stop them;
second, if they encounter even a slight emergency, one should hasten to their aid to rescue and protect them."
Third, one must not speak of private matters to others;
fourth, one should treat each other with mutual respect and deference;
fifth, whatever good things one possesses should be shared with others in proportion to their needs.
"Regarding those who bow toward the ground, this refers to a Great Officer (Dafu) looking after his slaves, guests, and servants; there are likewise five matters:
first, one should provide them with food and clothing at the proper times;
second, when they are sick or emaciated, one should summon a physician to treat them."
Third, one must not strike or beat them unjustly;
fourth, if they possess private property, one must not seize it;
fifth, when distributing goods, one must ensure they are treated with equality.
There are also five matters regarding how male and female servants should serve their masters:
first, they should rise early so as not to require the master to call them;
second, whatever tasks they must perform, they should carry them out with their own diligent attention.
Third, one must cherish the property of the great officers and must not discard it to give to beggars;
fourth, when the great officers enter or exit, one must escort them;
fifth, one must praise the virtues of the great officers and must not speak of their faults.
"Regarding those who pay homage to the heavens—that is, serving śramaṇas and practitioners—one should employ five matters:
first, approach them with a virtuous mind;
second, choose kind words with which to speak to them."
Third, one should honor them with one’s body;
fourth, one should cherish and long for them;
fifth, as śramaṇas and practitioners are heroes among men, one should respectfully serve them and inquire about the matters of transcending the world.
A śramaṇa or seeker of the Way should regard ordinary people with six intentions:
first, to teach them to practice giving, so that they do not become stingy or greedy;
second, to teach them to uphold the precepts, so that they do not violate the rules regarding sexual conduct.
Third, teach them patience so that they do not harbor resentment or anger;
fourth, teach them diligence so that they do not succumb to indolence or arrogance;
fifth, teach people single-mindedness so that they do not allow their minds to run wild.
Sixth, they teach others wisdom and must not themselves remain ignorant.
These śramaṇas and seekers of the Way instruct people to abandon evil and practice good, revealing the true path; their kindness is greater than that of one's own parents.
"If you practice in this way, you will be following your father's teaching of bowing in the six directions while he was alive; why then should you worry about not becoming wealthy?
Śīkhaṇḍī immediately received the five precepts, paid his respects, and departed.
The Buddha spoke these verses of praise:
"When the cock crows, rise early; Put on your robes and descend from the bed.
Wash and rinse to purify the mind, And with both hands, offer flowers and incense."
The Buddha, the Honored One, surpasses all devas; No ghosts or spirits can withstand him.
Bowing the head, one circumambulates the stupa and temple; With palms joined, one pays homage to the ten directions.
If a worthy person does not practice with diligence, They are like a tree without roots.
When the roots are severed and the branches and leaves fall, when will they ever join again?
Plucking flowers to place in the midday sun, how long can they remain fresh?
To let the mind loose and indulge its whims—once life has passed, what words can there be?
A person should contemplate impermanence; when death arrives, there is no fixed time.
To commit transgressions without self-awareness is to deceive oneself.
Now one shall enter hell; when will there be a time of release?
The wise receive the Buddha’s words; uphold the precepts and do not doubt them.
The Buddha is like a beautiful flowering tree, whom none fail to love and delight in.
Wherever the people hear of him, all rejoice.
When I attain Buddhahood, may I become like the Dharma King,
delivering all beings across birth and death so that none remain without liberation.
May the virtue of my precepts be a source of reliance, and may the rewards of my merit always follow me.
In this present life one becomes a leader of men, and in the end remains far from the three evil realms.
Through careful observance of the precepts, fear is dispelled; such merit and virtue are honored throughout the three worlds.
Ghosts, spirits, and the harms of malevolent poisons do not offend those who possess the precepts.
Falling into the mundane world brings the suffering of birth; life is as swift as a flash of lightning.
When the time for old age, sickness, and death arrives, no one can offer protection against its onset.
There is no kinsman to rely upon, and no place where one may hide.
Even celestial blessings have their end; how could human life be long-lasting?
One’s parents, home, and kin are like those of a traveler passing through.
When the lifespan ordained by past karma is exhausted, one must leave the old behind and undergo the new.
Each pursues their own past deeds, which are as boundless as a wheel;
arising and ceasing follow from sin and merit, the twelve links of birth and death.
Manifesting in this body, they roam free from turmoil, saving and nurturing all people.
Compassionately grieving for the multitudes fallen into various evils, And submerged in the deep abyss, you urge them forward with the six perfections;
Through cultivation, they attain spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, I bow my head in homage, Taking refuge in the God among Gods.
A human body is already difficult to obtain; having obtained it, one is further gripped by desire.
Greed and lust dwell within the consciousness, and painful perceptions bring no satisfaction.
One plants the seeds for future lives and joyfully departs for hell.
The six sense-faculties are fortunately complete; why do you bring yourself such distress?
If one can rectify the mind in all things, the deities of the three periods of time will be auspicious.
Without falling into the eight difficulties or the cravings of greed, one will follow their conduct as they are born throughout the ten directions.
Exerting diligence toward the realms of rebirth, Taking the six perfections as a bridge,
Extensively encouraging infinite wisdom, All are blessed by the divine light.
— The Sūtra on the Six Directions’ Salutation Spoken by the Buddha to Śakrāditya.
